stories.headline: US-IRAN CONFLICT ESCALATES, OIL SURGES TOWARD $94 BRENT
stories.body: The U.S. and Iran exchanged renewed strikes Tuesday, with U.S. forces hitting IRGC-linked targets after Iran attempted to mine the Strait of Hormuz and struck at sites in Jordan; Brent crude jumped more than 4% toward $94 a barrel while WTI rose 4.5% to nearly $90, reviving a war-risk premium in energy markets just as the Fed weighs a rate hike.
stories.explain: The Strait of Hormuz carries roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil, so any credible threat to transit gets priced into crude immediately, well before a single barrel is actually disrupted. That risk premium doesn't stay contained to energy — it feeds directly into near-term inflation expectations, which is exactly the channel through which today's oil spike reinforced bets on a September Fed hike and pressured both stocks and bonds.

stories.headline: FED RATE-HIKE ODDS JUMP TO 65% AS WARSH KEEPS HAWKISH TONE
stories.body: Futures markets now price roughly a 65% probability the Fed raises its target range by 25 bps to 3.75%-4.00% at the September meeting, up from about 35% before Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish remarks last Friday reiterating that the central bank has "work to do" on inflation. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed to around 4.78% on the repricing.
stories.explain: Fed funds futures translate a single official's language into a probability by pricing how the expected path of short-term rates shifts, so a hawkish word choice from the sitting chair can move odds by 30 points without a single data release changing. Because long-end Treasury yields embed that expected policy path plus a term premium, the same remarks pushed the 10-year higher immediately, raising the discount rate used to value future corporate cash flows — the direct link between Warsh's comments and today's equity selloff.

stories.headline: S&P 500 SLIDES 0.71%, NASDAQ 100 SHEDS NEARLY 2% AS TECH LEADS LOSSES
stories.body: The S&P 500 closed at 7,631.47, down 0.71%, while the Nasdaq 100 fell nearly 2% to roughly 28,868 as chip and mega-cap tech names absorbed the brunt of the selling. The Dow lost 419 points (-0.79%) to 52,766.88, with the pullback broad-based but concentrated most heavily in rate-sensitive growth stocks.
stories.explain: Growth and tech stocks carry a disproportionate share of their valuation in cash flows expected many years out, which makes their present value especially sensitive to the discount rate used to bring those flows back to today. When the 10-year yield jumps on hawkish Fed repricing, that discount rate rises and long-duration tech names get marked down harder than the broader index — precisely the pattern behind today's Nasdaq 100 underperformance relative to the S&P 500.

stories.headline: GOLD FALLS DESPITE WAR RISK AS RATE-HIKE BETS DOMINATE
stories.body: Gold slid roughly 1.8% to about $4,359 an ounce even as the U.S.-Iran conflict intensified — a break from its usual safe-haven script, as rising real yields tied to Fed rate-hike odds outweighed the geopolitical risk premium that would normally lift bullion.
stories.explain: Gold pays no yield, so its cost of carry is set by the real (inflation-adjusted) interest rate — when nominal yields rise faster than inflation expectations, real yields climb and holding zero-yield gold becomes relatively more expensive versus bonds. Today, that real-rate effect from the Fed repricing dominated the safe-haven bid the Iran escalation would normally generate, which is why gold and oil moved in opposite directions off the same headline.

stories.headline: MANUFACTURERS FLAG TARIFF AND ENERGY COST PRESSURE AS INPUT PRICES CLIMB
stories.body: Factory surveys this week show manufacturers citing rising input costs from tariffs, the AI-driven capex buildout, and now Middle East-driven energy prices as a growing squeeze on margins, adding another data point the Fed will weigh alongside oil-driven headline inflation ahead of its September decision.
stories.explain: Tariffs raise input costs directly, but the pass-through to consumer prices depends on how much of that cost businesses absorb versus pass along — when energy costs rise on top of tariffs, as they are now, firms have less margin cushion to absorb further shocks, which raises the odds both pressures show up together in the CPI print the Fed sees before its meeting.

stories.headline: KANSAS LANDS NO. 1 RECRUIT TYRAN STOKES AS 2026-27 PREVIEWS BEGIN
stories.body: Kansas secured a commitment from five-star forward Tyran Stokes, the No. 1 recruit in the 2026 class, as early way-too-early Top 25 rankings for 2026-27 begin to circulate. The move comes as the NCAA tournament field is set to expand from 68 to 76 teams starting this season.

stories.headline: CLIPPERS, RAPTORS IN TRADE TALKS FOR KAWHI LEONARD
stories.body: The Los Angeles Clippers and Toronto Raptors have been in extended discussions over a deal for All-NBA forward Kawhi Leonard as the league's offseason moves continue to reshape rosters. Elsewhere, DeMar DeRozan agreed to a one-year, $3.9 million deal with the Denver Nuggets, and Rockets guard Fred VanVleet opted into his $25 million option for 2026-27 as he returns from a torn ACL.

stories.headline: TEAMS FINALIZE 53-MAN ROSTERS AFTER WEEKEND CUTDOWN, 1,184 PLAYERS RELEASED
stories.body: All 32 teams trimmed to 53-man rosters by Sunday's deadline, with 1,184 players released leaguewide; the Titans cut QB Will Levis, leaving Cam Ward and Mitch Trubisky as Tennessee's only quarterbacks, while the defending champion Seahawks and the Patriots — set for a Super Bowl rematch on Sept. 9 — both finalized their rosters over the weekend.

stories.headline: WEEK 0 WRAPS WITH BELICHICK'S UNC UPSET OF TCU; MASSIVE WEEK 1 SLATE AHEAD
stories.body: Bill Belichick's North Carolina debut opened with a 15-10 win over TCU in Dublin, and No. 14 USC rolled past San Jose State, as Week 0 gave way to a 90-game Week 1 slate running Sept. 3-7 — headlined by Lane Kiffin's LSU debut against Clemson and No. 1 Ohio State hosting Ball State as a 50.5-point favorite.

sports.detail: Third-year coach Jedd Fisch's Huskies open the season at home vs. Washington State in the Apple Cup on Sept. 5, the first of four straight September home games at Husky Stadium as Washington enters its third season in the Big Ten.

Coming off a 16-17 (7-13 Big Ten) finish under Danny Sprinkle, Washington added Rutgers transfer Harun Zrno for 2026-27 after forward Hannes Steinbach was drafted by the Charlotte Hornets; regular season tips off in November.

The defending Super Bowl champions trimmed to 53 players over the weekend, waiving WR Julian Hicks, S Rodney Thomas II and others, while keeping just three healthy running backs as Zach Charbonnet recovers from ACL surgery; Seattle opens the season Sept. 9 at home against New England in a Super Bowl rematch.

Coming off a 60-win season, Detroit is still working out a long-term extension with center Jalen Duren as J.B. Bickerstaff enters his third season as coach; the Pistons play four preseason games before opening a higher-stakes 2026-27 campaign.
Seattle is at the Red Sox tonight at Fenway Park, first pitch 6:45 PM ET (4:45 PM MT) — the game is just getting underway as this brief publishes; check back for the result.

deepDive.title: From a Speech to 65%: How Fed Funds Futures Price a Rate Hike
content: Today's brief shows something that looks almost mechanical but isn't: a single set of hawkish remarks from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh moved the market-implied odds of a September rate hike from about 35% to roughly 65% within a few trading days, dragging the 10-year Treasury yield to 4.78%, hammering the Nasdaq 100 for a nearly 2% loss, and even flipping gold's usual safe-haven response upside down. None of that required a new inflation print or a formal Fed announcement — it came from futures contracts repricing off pure forward guidance.

Fed funds futures are contracts that settle based on the average effective fed funds rate over a given month, so their price today reflects the market's best guess of where that rate will land. Subtract the implied rate embedded in the contract from the current target, and you get an implied probability of a hike, cut, or hold at the next meeting — that math is exactly what produces a figure like today's 65%. Because these contracts trade continuously, they reprice within minutes of any Fed official's remarks, well before the actual policy decision, which is why Friday's comments moved markets on Tuesday with no new data in between.

This is the same mechanism that made the 2013 taper tantrum and the 2022 hiking cycle so violent: markets don't wait for the Fed to act, they front-run the expected path and adjust valuations immediately, which is why long-duration assets — long-dated Treasurys, high-multiple tech stocks, non-yielding gold — all move together on hawkish or dovish surprises even without any change in current policy. What most people miss is that the dot plot and futures-implied odds are related but separate signals: the dot plot shows what FOMC members themselves expect, while futures odds show what traders are willing to bet on, and the two can diverge sharply when the market thinks the Fed is bluffing or behind the curve.

For anyone watching this week's setup, the tell is this: as long as oil's Iran-driven spike keeps pushing headline inflation expectations higher, expect futures-implied hike odds to keep climbing into the FOMC meeting, dragging yields, tech valuations, and gold with them regardless of what the next CPI print actually shows. The real test comes with that report — if it comes in soft even with oil elevated, the odds could snap back down as fast as they rose, which is exactly the kind of two-sided volatility that makes trading rate expectations around a single speech a dangerous game.
